package_info.package_manager: Microsoft SQL Server (Extended Stored Procedure DLL)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (DLL-based, not versioned in a package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: The Maggie DLL is a backdoor that, once loaded as an Extended Stored Procedure in Microsoft SQL Server, enables attackers to execute arbitrary system commands, interact with the filesystem, brute-force logins to other MSSQL servers, create persistent backdoor users, and establish SOCKS5 proxies and TCP port forwarding. This provides attackers with full remote control, lateral movement, and covert network tunneling capabilities within the victim's environment.

execution_context.file_location: Loaded as an Extended Stored Procedure DLL in MSSQL server

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when triggered by a specially crafted SQL query, the code receives an arbitrary OS command as input, executes the command on the underlying operating system, captures the output, and returns the result to the attacker via the SQL response channel, enabling remote command execution and data exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Allowing arbitrary OS command execution from SQL queries is highly dangerous and enables attackers to fully compromise the host system, which is not a standard or safe feature of legitimate stored procedures.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal extended stored procedures should never provide unrestricted OS command execution to remote users, as this violates the principle of least privilege and exposes the server to complete takeover.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some administrative tools may allow limited, authenticated command execution for maintenance, but never in an unrestricted, unauthenticated, or remotely accessible manner.
key_indicators: Arbitrary command execution via SQL interface
No authentication or access control on command execution
Returns command output to remote user through SQL response
Direct mapping of SQL input to OS command execution

execution_context.file_location: Loaded as an Extended Stored Procedure DLL in MSSQL server

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when triggered by a SQL query, the code attempts to brute-force administrator logins on remote MSSQL servers using a list of credentials, and upon successful authentication, creates a new SQL user with hardcoded credentials to establish persistent unauthorized access.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Brute-forcing logins and creating unauthorized users are clear indicators of malicious lateral movement and persistence, as these actions are designed to expand attacker access and maintain control.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate stored procedures should not attempt to brute-force other servers or create unauthorized users, as this is outside the scope of any normal database operation and directly facilitates unauthorized access.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use for brute-forcing logins or creating hardcoded backdoor users in a production environment; such actions are always malicious in this context.
key_indicators: Automated brute-force of remote MSSQL servers from within a stored procedure
Creation of SQL users with hardcoded or suspicious credentials
Persistence mechanism via unauthorized user creation
No legitimate administrative or business purpose

execution_context.file_location: Loaded as an Extended Stored Procedure DLL in MSSQL server

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when triggered by a SQL query, the code starts a SOCKS5 proxy server on the infected MSSQL server, listens for incoming proxy connections, and forwards network traffic as directed by the attacker, enabling covert tunneling of arbitrary network traffic through the compromised host.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Enabling a SOCKS5 proxy on a database server is highly abnormal and facilitates covert lateral movement, data exfiltration, and network pivoting by attackers.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Database servers should not act as network proxies or bridgeheads, as this exposes internal networks to unauthorized access and bypasses network segmentation controls.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Proxies may be used for debugging in isolated test environments, but never on production database servers without strict controls and monitoring.
key_indicators: SOCKS5 proxy functionality embedded in a database extension
Database server listening on non-standard proxy ports
Network tunneling capability initiated via SQL commands
No legitimate business justification for proxy on database server

execution_context.file_location: Loaded as an Extended Stored Procedure DLL in MSSQL server

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when triggered by a SQL query, the code sets up a TCP port forwarding service on the infected server, listens on a specified port, and conditionally redirects incoming connections to a designated target IP and port if the source IP matches a user-specified mask, enabling covert access to internal network resources.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Port forwarding from a database server is highly unusual and enables attackers to bypass network segmentation, providing a stealthy bridge into protected network segments.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Database servers should not provide arbitrary port forwarding or act as network bridgeheads, as this undermines network security architecture.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Port forwarding may be used in controlled administrative scenarios, but never exposed via a backdoor or without strict authentication and monitoring.
key_indicators: Conditional TCP port forwarding initiated via SQL commands
Source IP mask for selective redirection
Database server acting as a network bridgehead
No legitimate administrative or business use for this functionality

attack_chain.action: Attacker uploads and loads the Maggie DLL as an Extended Stored Procedure on the MSSQL server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Backdoor is installed and ready to receive commands.

attack_chain.action: Attacker issues SQL queries to execute arbitrary OS commands via the backdoor.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains remote command execution on the server.

attack_chain.action: Attacker uses the backdoor to brute-force logins to other MSSQL servers and creates new backdoor users.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker achieves lateral movement and persistence in the environment.

attack_chain.action: Attacker enables SOCKS5 proxy or port forwarding to tunnel network traffic through the compromised server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker establishes covert network access to internal resources.

behavioral_signatures: Unusual invocation of extended stored procedures with command execution parameters (e.g., sp_maggie 'cmd', ...)
Creation of new SQL users with hardcoded or suspicious credentials from within stored procedures
MSSQL server initiating brute-force login attempts to other MSSQL servers over the network
Database server listening on unexpected ports associated with SOCKS5 proxy or port forwarding
Database server acting as a network proxy or bridgehead, relaying traffic to internal or external destinations
file_indicators: DLLs named sql64.dll or similar in MSSQL extension directories (e.g., C:\Program Files\Microsoft SQL Server\MSSQL\Binn\sql64.dll)
RAR SFX archives containing Maggie DLLs
network_indicators: Unexpected SOCKS5 or port forwarding traffic originating from MSSQL server
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for the loading of unknown or suspicious DLLs as extended stored procedures in MSSQL servers, especially those named sql64.dll or matching known malicious hashes. Alert on the creation of new SQL users with unusual or hardcoded credentials. Detect brute-force login attempts originating from MSSQL servers to other MSSQL instances. Monitor for unexpected network listeners (SOCKS5, port forwarding) or outbound connections to known malicious IPs/domains. Correlate file, network, and behavioral indicators to identify the presence of Maggie.
